passages.title: A model licence does not erase the dataset terms
passages.text:
A research consortium releases a collection of annotated engineering images to help universities study defects in manufactured components. The collection is accompanied by a licence that permits research and teaching use, requires attribution to the consortium and prohibits commercial use without a separate written permission. A start-up downloads the collection, trains a defect-detection model and later offers the model to factories on a paid subscription. The start-up argues that the model weights are its own work and that the original images are no longer visible in the finished product.

For this fictional problem, apply the following rule. A person who obtains material under a licence must comply with the conditions governing the use of that material. Permission to download or adapt a dataset for research does not automatically include permission to use it for commercial training. Attribution is a separate condition: naming the source does not cure a use that the licence prohibits. A user who wishes to move beyond the permitted purpose must obtain the required permission before doing so.

The rule also distinguishes the dataset from a model trained with it. The fact that a model's parameters are not ordinary copies of the original images does not, by itself, answer whether the training activity complied with the licence. That question concerns the use made of the dataset during development. Whether a particular model output reproduces protected material is a separate question that depends on the output and the applicable terms; it should not be assumed either that every output is restricted or that no output can raise a rights issue.

The consortium offers the start-up a route to seek a commercial licence. It asks the company to identify the version of the dataset used, describe the training purpose and explain whether the resulting model will be offered to paying customers. The start-up may continue using the images for non-commercial research within the original licence while the application is considered, but it must not treat the pending request as approval for commercial use. If permission is refused, it must stop the prohibited commercial use of the dataset and assess what steps are required for its existing service.

The rule does not prohibit commercial model development or require every research dataset to remain non-commercial forever. It requires a user to respect the scope of permission actually granted and to obtain new permission before crossing a material boundary. A developer's contribution to the model may be valuable, but it does not retrospectively expand the rights attached to the input material. The decisive issue is the permitted use of the dataset at the time it was used, not merely whether the final model contains a recognisable image.

passages.title: Consent for a new purpose
passages.text:
A learning application collects a student's name, class level and answers so that it can provide practice questions and record progress. When the application first launches, the student and parent are told that the information will be used to personalise learning and generate reports. Several months later, the provider decides to use the same data to build advertising profiles and share inferred interests with commercial partners. The original notice did not describe that purpose.

The provider's reuse of learning data is governed by a purpose-limitation rule. Personal information collected for a stated purpose may be used for that purpose and for uses that are reasonably necessary to provide it. A materially different use requires a clear explanation and a valid basis separate from the original permission. The fact that the information is already held does not make every later use permissible. Where consent is the chosen basis, the person must be able to understand the new purpose and make a genuine choice without being misled about the consequences of refusal.

The provider argues that advertising revenue will keep the learning service free. That may be a legitimate business objective, but it does not automatically make advertising profiles necessary to deliver practice questions. The provider could consider less intrusive options, such as contextual advertising that does not rely on an individual's learning history, a paid version or a separate optional feature. It must also consider whether a child or parent can realistically refuse the new use while continuing to access the core educational service.

If the application shares only aggregated statistics that cannot reasonably identify an individual, the analysis may differ. But replacing names with a code does not automatically make information anonymous if the provider or partner can reconnect the record to a student. The provider must examine the practical risk of re-identification and the information available to the recipient.

The rule distinguishes the original service purpose from a new commercial use. It does not prohibit a provider from developing additional features, but it requires the provider to explain the change and obtain the required basis before using existing information in a materially different way. Convenience and business value are not substitutes for a clear purpose and a meaningful choice.

If the provider relies on a statutory basis rather than consent for a particular use, it must still identify that basis and explain the relevant purpose where the rule requires notice. It cannot call a use optional in its public wording while making refusal impossible in practice. The actual design of the service therefore matters as much as the label placed on a button.

passages.title: A known software vulnerability and reasonable care
passages.text:
A company supplies software that stores medical appointment records for a network of clinics. During a routine security review, the company discovers a vulnerability that could allow an unauthorised user to access records if a particular configuration is left unchanged. A software update is available, but installing it requires the clinics to schedule a short maintenance window. The supplier delays informing the clinics because it fears that the announcement will damage confidence in the product.

The service contract imposes duties when the provider learns of a material security weakness. A service provider that knows of a material security vulnerability must take reasonable steps to reduce the risk and inform affected customers in time for them to protect their systems. The steps required depend on the seriousness of the vulnerability, the likelihood of exploitation, the sensitivity of the information and the availability of a safe remedy. A provider need not disclose technical details in a way that enables attackers to exploit the weakness, but it must give customers enough information to understand the risk and take appropriate action.

The rule also requires reasonable coordination. If an update may interrupt a critical service, the provider should explain the available maintenance options and support customers in applying the fix. It cannot treat operational inconvenience as a reason to leave a known serious vulnerability unaddressed. If exploitation is already suspected, the provider must assist with containment and preserve information needed to investigate the incident.

A clinic may have failed to install an earlier update, but that does not automatically release the supplier from its own duties. Responsibility may depend on the contract, the warnings previously given and the extent to which each party controlled the relevant configuration. The supplier should not assume that a customer's technical team can discover a vulnerability that the supplier has already identified internally.

The rule does not demand perfect security. It requires reasonable prevention, timely communication and cooperation in response to known risks. A provider that hides a serious weakness to protect reputation may increase harm to customers and patients. Security is an ongoing process, and the duty to act depends on what the provider knows and what practical steps are available.

The provider should also distinguish between a vulnerability that is merely theoretical and one that can be exploited under the customer's actual configuration. A risk notice can describe the affected versions, recommended mitigation and expected service interruption without publishing a step-by-step exploit. The rule requires enough information for protection, not instructions that create a new danger.

passages.title: A synthetic recording presented as genuine
passages.text:
A local election committee receives an audio recording in which a candidate appears to instruct supporters to damage a rival's campaign office. The recording is widely shared. A technical consultant says that the file contains signs of synthetic generation, while the person who supplied it insists that it is an authentic voice message. The committee must decide whether to rely on it when considering a complaint under its fictional conduct rules.

The committee evaluates digital recordings under an evidentiary standard focused on provenance and context. A recording may be considered as evidence only after the decision-maker examines its provenance, integrity and context. A file's apparent voice similarity is not enough to establish that the named person created or approved it. Relevant checks may include the original source, the chain of custody, signs of editing, metadata, corroborating evidence and whether the recording is complete. A technical assessment may assist, but its limitations must be disclosed.

The committee must give the person accused a fair opportunity to respond to the material relied upon. It may protect the identity of a witness where necessary, but should provide enough information about the allegation for a meaningful response. If the recording cannot be authenticated, the committee may consider other independent evidence; it cannot treat uncertainty as proof of guilt. Equally, a claim that a recording is synthetic does not automatically prove that it is false.

The rule does not require the committee to establish every technical detail beyond all doubt. It requires a reasoned assessment of reliability and a decision based on the total available evidence. If the consultant can identify likely manipulation but cannot determine who created it, the committee should state that limitation rather than attribute responsibility to a particular person without support.

The distinction between a file and the event it purports to record is central. Digital evidence can be persuasive because it appears precise and immediate, but its authenticity and context still require examination. The decision-maker remains responsible for explaining why the material is accepted, rejected or treated as inconclusive.

If the recording is circulated before the committee completes its review, the committee should avoid repeating the allegation as an established fact. It may issue a neutral notice that the material is being examined and remind participants not to harass either the candidate or the person who supplied the file. A precautionary response does not determine the final evidentiary question.

passages.title: A decision needs reasons that can be used
passages.text:
A public transport authority uses a model to decide which applicants qualify for discounted travel passes. A passenger receives a message stating that the application has been rejected because the applicant's “eligibility index” fell below the required threshold. The passenger cannot see which information produced the index and has no way to correct a mistaken address or income record.

The authority must follow a reasons-and-review standard when an automated tool affects access to a public service. Where a public authority makes an adverse decision that materially affects access to a public service, it must provide reasons sufficient for the affected person to understand the main basis of the decision and identify any relevant factual error. The authority need not publish its entire source code or disclose security-sensitive information. It must, however, explain the material categories considered and provide a route to challenge inaccurate or incomplete information.

The authority argues that a detailed explanation would make it easier for applicants to manipulate the system. The rule permits it to withhold narrow operational details where disclosure creates a demonstrated risk, but that concern cannot justify a message that gives no usable explanation at all. It may describe the relevant category, such as household income or residence, without revealing the precise detection threshold. An independent reviewer can examine whether the withheld detail is genuinely sensitive.

If the passenger shows that the address in the application was mistyped, the authority should correct the record and reconsider the decision. It need not grant the pass automatically if other eligibility conditions remain unsatisfied. The purpose of review is to ensure that the decision is based on accurate information and the published criteria, not to guarantee a favourable result.

The rule distinguishes an explanation that is technically detailed from one that is practically useful. A long report may reveal little if it does not identify the fact that affected the applicant. A concise notice can be adequate when it shows the relevant basis and tells the person how to correct it. The authority must remain able to explain the decision in terms that connect its model to the rules it is responsible for applying.

Reasons are also relevant to internal review. A second officer should be able to see which published criterion was applied and whether the underlying record was accurate. If the first officer cannot explain the result beyond repeating a score, the review process cannot test whether the model's output was used properly.

passages.title: Changing the rules of a digital platform
passages.text:
A digital marketplace publishes rules stating how sellers may list products, how complaints are investigated and when an account may be suspended. Small sellers rely on the platform to reach customers and plan stock purchases around the published fee schedule. The platform later changes its algorithm and begins charging a new visibility fee. It applies the change immediately to existing listings without notifying sellers or explaining how the fee affects product ranking.

The platform's terms include a fairness requirement for changes affecting existing sellers. A platform may revise its operating terms for legitimate business reasons, but a material change affecting existing users must be communicated clearly and with reasonable notice before it takes effect, unless an urgent security or legal reason requires immediate action. The platform must describe the practical effect of the change and provide a route for users to ask questions or close their account without being misled. A term that allows unlimited unilateral changes does not remove the obligation to act fairly.

The platform argues that sellers can leave whenever they wish. That option may be relevant, but it does not necessarily cure a sudden change after sellers have bought inventory or committed to advertising. A reasonable transition period allows users to adapt, cancel planned listings or compare alternatives. The required notice may depend on the magnitude of the change and the degree of reliance the platform could reasonably foresee.

If a security incident requires the platform to suspend a compromised account immediately, it may do so without the ordinary notice period. It should still provide a prompt explanation once disclosure is safe and allow the seller to challenge a mistaken identification. An urgent protective measure should not become a pretext for imposing an unrelated commercial term without notice.

The rule recognises that digital services need flexibility, but also that users organise real economic activity around platform rules. Fairness depends on the materiality of the change, the notice given, the ability to adapt and the reasons for any immediate action. The platform remains responsible for explaining how its published system has changed.

The platform should retain the earlier terms and the date on which each version applied. If a seller complains that a new fee was applied before notice, the record can show what the seller was told and when. Version control does not decide whether a change is fair, but it makes the decision easier to examine.

passages.title: Benchmark performance and deployment risk
passages.text:
A technology agency reports that a new language model achieved a higher score than its predecessor on a set of standardised reasoning tests. The agency concludes that the new model is safer for use in public services because it makes fewer errors on the benchmark. The report is based on thousands of test questions and has been reviewed by an external laboratory.

The improvement is meaningful within the limits of the test. However, the benchmark contains short, clearly stated questions and does not reproduce the conditions under which people approach a public service. A user may provide incomplete information, use a regional language, describe a problem indirectly or ask for help while under stress. The system may also be connected to databases or tools that introduce errors not present in the benchmark.

A second issue concerns the nature of the errors. A model may improve its average score by answering more common questions correctly while continuing to fail on a small group of high-consequence cases. If the agency uses the model to explain benefit eligibility, a wrong answer about an appeal deadline may matter more than several correct answers about general information. A single average score hides the distribution and seriousness of mistakes.

The agency proposes a staged trial. It will test the model on realistic enquiries, compare performance across languages and user groups, measure the frequency of harmful errors and keep a human officer responsible for final decisions. It will also record cases where users abandon the interaction or seek help elsewhere. The benchmark score remains one part of the evidence, not the final test of suitability.

The report's conclusion is therefore stronger than its data justify. Better benchmark performance is evidence of progress on the tasks measured. It does not automatically establish safety in every deployment. A responsible evaluation asks whether the test resembles actual use, whether errors are distributed fairly and whether the institution can detect and correct failures after release.

The agency could also test whether the model's advantage persists when questions are asked in languages and formats that were underrepresented in its benchmark. A deployment evaluation should include users who need assistive technology and people who provide partial information. If the model performs well only for a narrow test population, the headline improvement may not transfer to the public service.

passages.title: Offline alternatives and resilience
passages.text:
A city replaces paper appointment slips at public clinics with a mobile application. Within six months, online bookings rise and the average time spent at the registration counter falls. The health department concludes that the digital system has made access more efficient and proposes closing the remaining walk-in desk at smaller clinics.

The figures describe users who successfully booked online. They do not reveal how many people tried and failed, how many lacked a compatible phone or how often the network was unavailable. In neighbourhoods with reliable connectivity, the application may reduce waiting. In remote areas, a resident may travel to a clinic only to learn that the booking system cannot verify an identity record. A lower counter queue does not necessarily mean that fewer people were unable to obtain an appointment.

The department argues that maintaining a walk-in desk is expensive and that most residents now own a smartphone. Ownership alone does not prove that a person can complete a form, receive a one-time password or understand an error message. A phone may be shared by several family members, or the data connection may be unavailable at the time the appointment is needed. A system that assumes continuous access may work well in ordinary conditions and fail precisely when demand is high.

A more complete evaluation would measure successful appointment completion across channels, not only online submissions. It would also record failed attempts, abandoned journeys and the use of assisted booking. The department could maintain a smaller assisted desk or an offline queue that syncs records when connectivity returns. That arrangement would retain most of the digital efficiency while providing a fallback for people excluded by the technology.

The question is not whether digital services are preferable to paper in every case. It is whether the system remains usable when devices, connectivity or identity records fail. Resilience includes the capacity to continue serving people during disruption. A channel that disappears when its supporting infrastructure fails should not be treated as the only measure of successful modernisation.

The department should also compare the cost of assisted access with the cost of failed appointments. An offline route may appear less efficient when measured as staff time per booking, but it can prevent a person from making repeated journeys after a digital failure. The proper comparison includes successful access, not simply the cost of processing a completed online form.

passages.title: More data can reduce trust
passages.text:
A municipal safety unit installs additional cameras and proposes linking their footage with travel-card records to identify crowding and respond to emergencies. Officials argue that more information will allow faster decisions and reduce the risk of missing a dangerous incident. The system is expected to help planners understand how people move through crowded spaces.

A civil-society group agrees that accurate information can improve safety but questions whether every data source is necessary. The unit has not shown that linking individual travel histories is required to estimate crowd density. It could use aggregated counts or short retention periods for much of the planning work. Linking identifiable records may create a detailed history of a person's movements that could later be used for unrelated purposes.

The unit replies that safeguards can be added after launch. Yet trust depends partly on what people understand before data collection begins. If residents believe that every journey is being recorded without a clear purpose, they may avoid public transport or change their behaviour. That response can make the data less representative and undermine the very planning objective the unit wants to support.

A pilot could compare several methods. One would use camera-based counts that do not identify individuals; another would link records only for a limited emergency investigation under a defined authorisation process. The unit could measure response time, false alerts, retention needs and public understanding. It should explain what information is collected, who can access it and when it is deleted. The choice should be based on evidence of necessity and effectiveness rather than the assumption that more data always produces better decisions.

The safety objective is legitimate, but it does not settle the scope of collection. More information may improve a system when it is relevant and reliable. Unnecessary collection can increase risk, cost and public resistance. A successful design must consider both operational performance and the conditions that make people willing to use a public service.

The unit could also publish a retention schedule and an audit record of who accessed identifiable footage. Independent review may help determine whether the safety benefit justifies the collection and whether less intrusive information would have achieved the same result. These safeguards will not remove every concern, but they allow the public to examine whether the stated purpose is being respected.

passages.title: An explanation must permit correction
passages.text:
A university deploys an automated system to identify students who may need additional academic support. It sends a notice when a student's activity falls below a threshold and recommends a meeting with an adviser. The university describes the system as supportive rather than punitive, and says students can contact the office if they disagree with the result.

Students soon discover that the notice does not identify which activity triggered it. One student had completed assignments offline during a platform outage; another had changed courses and was no longer required to use the earlier online module. Both received the same notice. The university's staff could see the score but not a clear explanation of the inputs that determined it.

The university argues that showing a detailed explanation may reveal how to avoid detection. But the purpose is to offer support, not to catch misconduct. A student who does not know whether the notice concerns attendance, course registration or assignment submission cannot correct the relevant record. The general invitation to contact the office places the burden on the student to guess what went wrong.

A revised process shows the categories contributing to the alert and the date of the records used. Students can correct a course enrolment or report a platform outage. Advisers review the corrected information before recommending support. The university still protects technical details that would compromise system security, but it no longer treats a score as a sufficient explanation.

The change does not require every automated system to reveal every internal calculation. It requires a level of explanation that matches the purpose and impact of the system. Where the institution expects people to act on a notice, it must give them enough information to understand what is being asked and to correct a material error. Without that possibility, the promise of supportive intervention may become an unexplained label attached to the student.

The institution should also tell the student how long a correction request is expected to take and what happens while it is being considered. A route that exists only on paper may not help someone who needs support immediately. Practical contestability therefore includes a reachable contact, a reasonable response time and a way to avoid an adverse label while a material record error is being checked. A correction can be simple, but the process should remain visible.

passages.title: Shared AI compute allocation
passages.text: A public research centre has 1,200 accelerator-hours available in one week. University A receives 35%, University B receives 25% and start-up teams share the remainder. Of the start-up allocation, 40% is reserved for safety testing and the rest for general research. During the week, University A uses 90% of its allocation and University B uses 80%. The centre charges ₹500 per used accelerator-hour for external users. Treat all percentages as exact and ignore taxes.

passages.title: Digital wallet transaction study
passages.text:
A payment network processes 80,000 transactions in a month. Forty-five per cent are small-merchant payments, 30% are bill payments and the remainder are person-to-person transfers. Of small-merchant payments, 4% are reversed; of bill payments, 2% are reversed; and 1% of person-to-person transfers are reversed. A separate audit finds 600 transactions requiring manual review. Assume the three transaction categories are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

The network's finance team reports reversals separately from the manual-review count. A transaction may be reversed without requiring manual review, and a transaction flagged for review may ultimately be valid. Do not assume that the two groups are identical or add them together unless a question explicitly asks for their combined total.

passages.title: Cyber incident response
passages.text: A service provider receives 2,400 security alerts in a quarter. Thirty per cent are classified as high priority, 45% as medium priority and the remainder as low priority. Analysts resolve 80% of high-priority alerts, 75% of medium-priority alerts and 90% of low-priority alerts within the target time. Each resolved high-priority alert requires an average of 3 analyst-hours, each medium alert 1.5 hours and each low alert 0.5 hour. Assume the stated percentages are exact.
